rows: Work near overhead electric lines must be carefully planned to avoid danger.
Close approach can cause a flashover even without direct contact.
Overhead lines should be assumed live unless the owner confirms otherwise.
Line routes should be identified before plant, materials or work enter the area.
Avoidance, diversion or isolation should be considered before relying on work controls.
Barriers, goalposts and warning notices may be needed where access passes beneath lines.
Safe clearance information should be obtained from the line owner.
High or long plant requires supervision and physical or procedural limits where necessary.
A map line or visual estimate does not establish a safe clearance.
Task conclusions require exact line position, voltage, owner advice, plant reach, access, controls and supervision evidence.
All roof work should be organised and planned so it is carried out safely.
Roof work is high risk even when the task lasts only a few minutes.
Workers must be trained, competent and instructed in the required precautions.
A method statement is commonly used to communicate roof-work controls.
Safe access to and from the roof must be provided.
Roof edges and openings require suitable protection.
Fragile areas must be identified and controlled.
Clients and contractors should coordinate arrangements on occupied business premises.
A roof type or short task duration does not prove that work is low risk.
Task conclusions require access, edge protection, fragility, weather, rescue, competence and supervision evidence.
Work on or near fragile surfaces should be avoided where possible.
Roofs should be treated as fragile until a competent person confirms otherwise.
Rooflights and corroded sheets can be difficult to recognise as fragile.
Where avoidance is impossible, suitable staging and collective fall protection are required.
Fall restraint, fall arrest or safety nets may supplement collective controls.
Warning notices should be fixed on approaches to fragile surfaces.
Workers need training and instruction in the required precautions.
Clients and contractors should cooperate on occupied premises.
A material description or old survey does not prove current load-bearing capacity.
Conclusions require competent assessment, condition, access, staging, edge protection, fall systems and rescue evidence.
Demolition work must be planned and managed as construction work.
Clients should appoint designers and contractors with relevant skills, knowledge and experience.
Pre-construction information should include structural, asbestos and service information.
A competent person should prepare the demolition method.
The method should address the structure, site hazards and chosen sequence.
Stability and debris should be controlled throughout the work.
Exclusion and debris zones should reflect the demolition technique and changing conditions.
Workers must be supervised and follow the approved plan.
A demolition plan or contractor appointment does not prove that live work remains safe.
Site conclusions require surveys, sequence, stability, plant, services, exclusion zones, debris and supervision evidence.
